item.question: The two triangles ABC and XYZ are congruent and lie at different tilts. Which corners should be placed on each other so that the equal sides overlap? Are there other ways of overlapping them so that they fit exactly?
steps: Find the shortest side of each triangle, the one with a single bar. These two sides must land on each other.
Their end corners must land on each other too. Take the next side of each, with two bars, and then the last side, with three bars, and check the same way.
The corners that land on each other are A on X, B on Y and C on Z.
The three sides of each triangle are all different, so every side has only one partner. Any other pairing puts a long side on a short one and leaves an end sticking out.
Because A sits on X, B on Y and C on Z, angle A equals angle X, angle B equals angle Y and angle C equals angle Z. Nobody had to measure them.
item.answer: Place A over X, B over Y and C over Z. There is no other way, because the three sides are all different. The angles are equal as a result: angle A = angle X, angle B = angle Y, angle C = angle Z.

item.question: The congruence of two triangles is written as ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ. Why does the order of the letters matter? Is ΔACB ≅ ΔXYZ a correct way to write the same fact, and is ΔACB ≅ ΔXZY?
steps: Read ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ as an instruction: the first letters go together, the second letters go together and the third letters go together. A lands on X, B on Y and C on Z.

Read ΔACB ≅ ΔXYZ the same way. The first letters give A on X. The second letters give C on Y, and the third letters give B on Z. That is a different matching from the real one, so a long side would be laid on a short side.
Read ΔACB ≅ ΔXZY. The first letters give A on X, the second letters give C on Z, and the third letters give B on Y. These are exactly the pairs of the real matching.
The left side was shuffled and the right side was shuffled the same way, so the message did not change.
item.answer: The order of the letters is the matching. ΔACB ≅ ΔXYZ gives a different matching and does not describe how the triangles land. ΔACB ≅ ΔXZY keeps the same matching and is a correct way to write it. Shuffle both sides alike, or neither.

item.question: A rectangle ABCD is cut along the diagonal BD. Can you identify a pair of congruent triangles in it? Why are they congruent?
steps_tex: Pull the two triangles apart: triangle $ABD$ on one side and triangle $CDB$ on the other.
$AB = CD$ and $AD = CB$, because opposite sides of a rectangle are equal. Two pairs of sides match.
$BD$ is a side of both triangles. It is the same line, so it is equal to itself: a free side.
All three pairs of sides match, so the triangles are congruent by the side side side condition.

item.question: Can the correspondence be A with C, B with B, D with D? Which correspondence is correct, and how do you write the congruence?
steps_tex: Follow A with $C$ and $B$ with $B$. That lays side $AB$ onto side $CB$.
$AB$ and $CB$ are not equal, so one hangs over and the matching does not fit.
Start from the sides instead. $AB$ is equal to $CD$, $AD$ is equal to $CB$ and $BD$ is equal to $DB$, so A lands on $C$, $B$ lands on $D$ and $D$ lands on $B$.
Write the corners in that order: triangle $ABD$ is congruent to triangle $CDB$.
item.answer_tex: No, that matching lays $AB$ onto $CB$ and those sides are not equal. The correct correspondence is A with $C$, $B$ with $D$, $D$ with $B$, so triangle $ABD \cong$ triangle $CDB$. Shuffling both names the same way, for example $ADB \cong CBD$, says the same thing.

item.question: Instead of measuring three sides, can the three angles recreate the triangle exactly? Try angles of 30, 70 and 80 degrees.
steps: Draw a base of any length. Make an angle of 30 degrees at one end and 70 degrees at the other, and let the two lines meet at the top.
The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees, so the third angle is 180 - 30 - 70 = 80 degrees. It is forced, not chosen.
The base was never fixed. Draw it short, longer and longest, and each time the angles are 30, 70 and 80 degrees.
The three triangles have the same shape but different sizes, so a tracing of the smallest does not land on the largest.
So many triangles fit these three angles and they are not congruent. Angles alone do not pin the triangle down.
item.answer: No. Many triangles of different sizes have angles of 30, 70 and 80 degrees, so three angles are not enough to recreate a triangle exactly.

3. The base was never fixed. Draw it short, longer and longest, and each time the angles are 30, 70 and 80 degrees.
4. The three triangles have the same shape but different sizes, so a tracing of the smallest does not land on the largest.
5. So many triangles fit these three angles and they are not congruent. Angles alone do not pin the triangle down.
Answer: No. Many triangles of different sizes have angles of 30, 70 and 80 degrees, so three angles are not enough to recreate a triangle exactly.

item.question: Two triangles have AB = XY = 6 cm, AC = XZ = 5 cm and angle A = angle X = 30 degrees. Are they congruent? Construct a triangle with these measurements and compare it with the triangles your classmates draw.
steps: Draw AB = 6 cm. At A, measure 30 degrees from AB and draw AC = 5 cm along that line.
Join B and C. The closing side BC is about 3 cm, and calculation gives 3.006 cm.
Everyone who follows these three instructions gets the same BC, because the two arms and the opening between them leave only one place for the tips.
Lay a tracing of one triangle over another: they land exactly. There cannot be a non-congruent triangle with these measurements.
The rule is called S A S, side, angle, side. The angle sits between the two sides, so it is the included angle.
item.answer: Yes. Two sides and the angle between them fix the triangle, so the two triangles are congruent. The closing side is about 3 cm for every child.

item.question: Construct a triangle with PQ = 6 cm, the angle at P equal to 30 degrees and a side of 4 cm from Q. The angle is not between the two given sides. Can there be triangles that are not congruent with these measurements?
steps: Draw the base PQ of 6 cm, and at P make an angle of 30 degrees. Run a long line l out from P.
Open a compass to 4 cm, put its point on Q and swing an arc across the line l.
The arc cuts the line l at two different points, R and S.
Triangle PQR and triangle PQS both have PQ = 6 cm, an angle of 30 degrees at P and a side of 4 cm from Q.

The straight distance from Q down to the line l is 6 x sin 30 degrees = 3 cm. The swinging side is 4 cm, which is longer than 3 cm so it reaches the line, and shorter than 6 cm so it reaches twice, at 2.55 cm and 7.84 cm from P.
Two triangles that are not congruent obey all three measurements, so two sides and an angle not between them (SSA) do not guarantee congruence.
item.answer: Yes. The arc cuts the line at two points, giving two different triangles with the same measurements, so SSA does not guarantee congruence. Sometimes the loose side reaches the line only once, but you cannot tell without checking.
